title: The Mirror Number
subtitle: Reverse half, compare once.
description: Check whether an integer is a palindrome without converting it to a string — reverse only half the digits.
prompt: Determine whether a non-negative-integer-or-negative input reads the same forwards and backwards — without any string conversion. Print `yes` or `no`.
instructions: Print `yes` if it is a palindrome, otherwise `no`.
constraints: No string conversion of the number.

examples.title: Example 1
examples.explanation: Reversed half (12…21) matches the rest (123 → 12 | 3). Yes.

examples.title: Example 2
examples.explanation: Ends in zero but is not zero — cannot be a palindrome.

hints: You never need more than half the digits.
Odd-length palindromes have a middle digit that matches anything — drop it.

solution.summary: Reject negatives and non-zero multiples of ten. Then reverse digits while the reversed half is still smaller than the rest; at the end compare equal (even length) or reversed/10 === rest (odd length).
approach: Early exits: n < 0 → no; n % 10 === 0 && n !== 0 → no.
Loop while rest > reversed: peel a digit onto reversed.
Compare reversed === rest (even digit count) or reversed/10 === rest (odd, drop the middle digit).

code.label: Reference solution

commonMistakes: Reversing the entire number and risking overflow in fixed-width languages.
Forgetting that 0 is a palindrome while 10, 100, 1000 never are.
